input: A flat stainless steel wall with a thickness of 12 mm separates two process streams, and the goal here is to estimate the heat flux passing through it. The thermal conductivity of the wall material is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, while the measured temperature difference across the wall is 325 K. Under conditions of steady, one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through a plane wall increases in proportion to the temperature difference and decreases in inverse proportion to the thickness of the wall, and applying this relationship to the values given yields a heat flux of 433333 W m⁻². It is important to note that this estimate deliberately excludes the surface, or film, resistances on either side of the wall. Because those resistances would act in series with the resistance of the metal itself, including them would lower the overall flux, since a portion of the temperature difference would then be consumed across the fluid films instead of across the wall. The figure should therefore be understood as the value for conduction through the metal alone, under the simplifying assumptions of a linear temperature profile, constant conductivity, and negligible edge losses and contact resistance at the faces of the wall.
target:
Calculate the heat flux through a flat stainless steel wall of thickness 12 mm that separates two process streams. The wall has thermal conductivity 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 325 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction through a plane wall gives a heat flux proportional to the temperature difference and inversely proportional to the thickness; for a thin metal wall the temperature profile is taken as linear, and the flux is uniform over the wall area. Substitution of the stated values gives a heat flux of 433333 W m⁻².

The estimate excludes surface (film) resistances on the two faces of the wall. Film resistances act in series with the conduction resistance, and including them lowers the flux, because part of the temperature difference then falls across the fluid films rather than across the metal. The stated flux is the conduction-only value for the wall itself, and a figure for the stream-to-stream transfer would sit below it by an amount set by the two film coefficients, which the estimate does not use. The calculation treats the conductivity as constant over the temperature range of the wall; a conductivity that varies with temperature would change the profile from linear to curved and would change the flux at the same terminal temperatures. Heat loss through the edges of the wall is neglected, as is any contact resistance at the faces.
